data_notes: Thematic source: mahalle_population_2024.geojson (İzmir mahalle polygons, population 2024)
Flow source: tire_mahalle_upi_sosyoekonomik.gpkg (assembly areas + critical assets)
DEM reprojected from EPSG:4326 to EPSG:32635 (the ridge engine needs map units)
OD table: 900 real origin→critical-asset pairs (distance-decay gravity on real capacities)

quick_style.params:
INPUT            = İzmir mahalle (2024)
FIELD            = pop_density
MODE             = 1
CLASSES          = 5
METHOD           = 2
PALETTE          = 15
REVERSE          = False
OUTLINE          = True
MONOCHROME       = False
quick_style.notes:
Classes are equal-count by default, so every band holds the same
number of neighbourhoods — good for comparison, poor for showing
absolute gaps. Switch to Geometric interval when the density
distribution is long-tailed (it always is, in a real city).

The renderer is applied to the INPUT layer in place: save the
layer afterwards (Layer ▸ Save As ▸ GeoPackage) to keep the style.

quick_style_monochrome.params:
INPUT            = İzmir mahalle (2024)
FIELD            = pop_density
MODE             = 1
CLASSES          = 5
METHOD           = 2
PALETTE          = 21
REVERSE          = False
OUTLINE          = True
MONOCHROME       = True
quick_style_monochrome.notes:
Monochrome swaps the colour ramp for black-and-white hatch and dot
patterns that darken with the value — photocopy-safe and
journal-safe. The legend still carries the numbers, so nothing is
lost in greyscale.

Use this whenever the deliverable will be printed in black and
white or photocopied.

normalize_field.params:
INPUT            = İzmir mahalle (2024)
FIELD            = pop_total
METHOD           = 0
DENOMINATOR      = pop_15_64
SCALE            = 1000.0
PALETTE          = 15
CLASSES          = 5
normalize_field.notes:
Rate = pop_total ÷ pop_15_64 gives residents per 1 000 working-age
people. This is the dependency indicator: values above 1 mean a
neighbourhood depends on people outside its own working-age group.

Always normalize before classifying. A raw population choropleth
mostly redraws the urban footprint.

classification.params:
INPUT            = İzmir mahalle (2024)
FIELD            = pop_density
CLASSES          = 5
METHOD           = 0
PALETTE          = 15
classification.notes:
Adaptive Geometric Interval (GIC) starts from a geometric progression
of class widths and merges classes until the variance criterion is
met — it follows the shape of skewed urban data instead of
forcing equal counts.

Compare with Fisher-Jenks: GIC keeps a readable, ordered set of
round-ish intervals; Jenks minimises within-class variance.

bivariate.params:
INPUT            = İzmir mahalle (2024)
FIELD_X          = elderly_share
FIELD_Y          = child_share
CLASSES          = 3
METHOD           = 0
PALETTE_PRESET   = 2
COLOR_LL         = #eff3ff
COLOR_LH         = #bdd7e7
COLOR_HL         = #fdbb84
COLOR_HH         = #e34a33
bivariate.notes:
Each polygon carries a class label combining an X band and a Y band
(bivar_class). The 3×3 palette therefore reads on two axes at once.

X axis = share of residents aged 65+, Y axis = share aged 0–14.
Upper-left = old and few children (care load), upper-right = old
and young (care load plus school load) — the hardest quadrant.

Bivariate Legend Matrix (3x3)

Y: 0-14 yaş payı  |  X: 65+ yaş payı

High1,32,33,3
Medium1,22,23,2

bivariate_matrix.notes:
The legend is exported as vector geometry (diamonds or squares) and
as standalone HTML, so it can be dropped into a layout or a
manuscript without re-drawing the matrix by hand.

Keep the axis labels identical to the map caption — the matrix is
meaningless without them.

value_by_alpha.params:
INPUT            = İzmir mahalle (2024)
FIELD_COLOUR     = pop_density
FIELD_ALPHA      = working_share
ALPHA_MIN        = 64
ALPHA_MAX        = 255
PALETTE          = 5
CLASSES          = 5
value_by_alpha.notes:
Hue carries the value (population density); opacity carries the
reliability proxy (share of the working-age population).

Faded polygons are not missing data — they are uncertain data.
That distinction is the whole point of Value-by-Alpha: a normal
choropleth would hide them behind a 'no data' colour.

cartogram.params:
INPUT            = İzmir ilçeleri
FIELD            = pop_total
MAX_ITERATIONS   = 60
MAX_ERROR        = 5.0
PALETTE          = 1
ITERATIONS       = 60
RESIDUAL_ERROR   = 4.4972432621029514e+18
cartogram.notes:
Every polygon is resized so that its AREA is proportional to the
value, while the shared borders stay contiguous.

Compare panel 1 with panel 3: the eastern mountain districts
shrink, the central districts swell. The residual error (%) tells
you how close the engine got to the target areas.

dorling.params:
INPUT            = İzmir ilçeleri
FIELD            = pop_total
SIZE_FACTOR      = 1.0
ATTRACTION       = 0.6
GAP              = 3.0
ITERATIONS       = 300
PALETTE          = 0
ROUNDS           = 316
RESIDUAL         = 0.00242618183044963
dorling.notes:
Circles replace polygons: area is proportional to the value, but
the circle stays near its original position.

Use Dorling when the SHAPE of the unit carries meaning (coastline,
river, border) and you still need to show totals. Use a continuous
cartogram when the shape itself is the message.

dot_density.params:
INPUT            = İzmir mahalle (2024)
FIELD            = pop_total
VALUE_PER_DOT    = 500.0
DOT_SIZE         = 2.0
DOT_COLOR        = #7c3aed
SEED             = 42
dot_density.notes:
One dot represents VALUE_PER_DOT residents. The dots are seeded, so
re-running with the same SEED gives the identical map — essential
for a report where the figure must be reproducible.

Dots are placed inside the polygon and never in holes, so the map
shows where people actually are, not a scatter of centroids.

proportional_symbols.params:
INPUT            = İzmir mahalle noktaları
FIELD            = pop_total
MAX_SIZE         = 14.0
MIN_SIZE         = 2.0
SHAPE            = 0
FILL_COLOR       = #e38e4f
OUTLINE_COLOR    = #7c2d12
FLANNERY         = True
proportional_symbols.notes:
Flannery compensation corrects the perceptual under-estimation of
area differences: a circle that looks twice as big is not twice
the value.

Use proportional symbols when the values live at points (centres,
stations) and the polygons would carry no extra information.

hexbin.params:
INPUT            = İzmir mahalle noktaları
CELL_SIZE        = 1500.0
WEIGHT           = pop_total
STAT             = 1
PALETTE          = 5
CLASSIFIER       = 0
CLASSES          = 5
hexbin.notes:
The point layer is binned into a pointy-top hexagonal grid — the
aggregation that avoids the overplotting of raw points.

Here the weight (population) is SUMMED per cell, so the map reads
as 'how many people live in each hexagon'. The grid also removes
the false precision of small-area administrative units.

label_points.notes:
Each polygon gets an anchor at its pole of inaccessibility — the
point furthest from the polygon edge, which is guaranteed to lie
inside the shape.

Centroid labels drift off concave shapes; these do not. Join this
layer to your label layer to place district names safely.

graticule.params:
EXTENT           = ….1852393625,4359618.902638675 [EPSG:32635]
X_INTERVAL       = 10000.0
Y_INTERVAL       = 10000.0
LINE_STYLE       = 1
LINE_COLOR       = #64748b
LINE_WIDTH       = 0.35
graticule.notes:
Meridians and parallels are placed on a round interval and each one
carries its own coordinate label.

Use a 10 km interval on a city-scale map, 1° on a country map.
The graticule is a reference layer — always draw it beneath the
data, in a low-contrast grey.

ridge_map.params:
RASTER           = dem_utm35n
N_LINES          = 120
VERTICAL_SCALE   = 3.868
LINE_SPACING     = 0.0
SMOOTH           = 2.0
EXTENT           = …5.625940838,4252875.625940838 [EPSG:32635]
LINE_COLOR       = #111827
LINE_WIDTH       = 0.28
ridge_map.notes:
The raster is sampled along scanlines and every scanline is drawn
as a profile: elevation becomes a stack of ridgelines.

Vertical exaggeration is the parameter that matters — too little and
the relief disappears, too much and it becomes a cartoon. Change
VERTICAL_SCALE and compare.

building_25d.params:
INPUT            = osm_buildings
HEIGHT_FIELD     = height_m
HEIGHT_MODE      = 0
FLOOR_HEIGHT     = 3.5
RENDER_MODE      = 0
FLOOR_PALETTE    = 0
MAX_FLOORS       = 12
PRESET           = 0
ANGLE            = 45.0
HEIGHT_SCALE     = 1.0
MAX_HEIGHT       = 60.0
STEPPED          = False
STEP_HEIGHT      = 3.5
SHADOW_ENABLED   = True
SHADOW_SPREAD    = 1.2
WALL_SHADING     = True
SUMMARY          = 02CartoLab 2.5D style applied · Layer: osm_buildings · Height field: height_m · Height source: height · Render
building_25d.notes:
The height field drives a native QGIS 25d renderer: roofs, walls and
directional shading. The plugin writes the style as a reusable
expression, so the same rule works on any layer with the same
height field.

MAX_HEIGHT clamps outliers; without it one 300 m tower flattens
every other building in the frame.

flow_map.params:
ZONES            = OD zones
ZONE_ID          = zone_id
FLOWS            = OD table
ORIGIN           = origin_id
DEST             = dest_id
VOLUME           = flow_vol
DIRECTED         = True
MIN_VOLUME       = 5.0
TOP_N            = 0
CURVATURE        = 0.32
MAX_WIDTH        = 4.0
MIN_WIDTH        = 0.25
END_GAP          = 6.0
ARROWS           = True
PALETTE          = 0
flow_map.notes:
Each record becomes a curved desire line between the two zone
anchors. Width is proportional to the volume; large flows are drawn
first so small flows stay visible on top.

DIRECTED keeps the arrowheads and separates A→B from B→A. Arrows
are the difference between a flow map and a network diagram.
